methods.label: Use distances from the common center
methods.explanation:
Assume the intended symmetric circumscription: each tetrahedron face touches the three balls adjacent to that face. We will calculate its edge length, then explain why this tangency assumption matters.

The centers of the four unit balls are pairwise \(2\) units apart, so they form a regular tetrahedron of edge \(2\). We need the distances from a regular tetrahedron's center to its faces and vertices.

For a regular tetrahedron of edge \(L>0\), an equilateral face has vertex-to-center distance \(L/\sqrt3\), obtained by taking two thirds of its altitude. Its tetrahedron height is therefore
\[
H=\sqrt{L^2-\frac{L^2}{3}}
=L\sqrt{\frac23}.
\]
By symmetry, the common center lies on this altitude. If its distance above the base is \(z\), equating its squared distances to the top vertex and a base vertex gives
\[
(H-z)^2=z^2+\frac{L^2}{3}.
\]
Using \(H^2=2L^2/3\) yields \(z=H/4\). Thus the center-to-face distance \(\rho\) and center-to-vertex distance \(R\) are
\[
\rho=\frac{L\sqrt6}{12},
\qquad
R=\frac{L\sqrt6}{4}.
\]
For the tetrahedron of ball centers, these distances are \(\rho_0=\sqrt6/6\) and \(R_0=\sqrt6/2\).

Under the assumed three-ball contact on each face, that face is parallel to the plane through the three corresponding centers and lies one unit farther outward. The outer tetrahedron therefore has center-to-face distance \(\rho_0+1\), giving
\[
\frac{s\sqrt6}{12}=\frac{\sqrt6}{6}+1.
\]
Hence
\[
s=\boxed{2+2\sqrt6},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{E}\) under the stated assumption.

The contact pattern is essential if circumscription means only an enclosing tetrahedron with tangent faces. Reflect the outer tetrahedron's orientation through the common center, and resize it so that its center-to-face distance is \(R_0+1\). Each face center now lies on a ray through one ball center. The gap from that ball center to the face is exactly \(1\), so the face is tangent to that ball. The other three centers lie in a perpendicular plane on the far side of the common center, so their balls are farther inside that face. This construction encloses all four balls and has edge
\[
s'=\frac{12(R_0+1)}{\sqrt6}
=6+2\sqrt6.
\]
The floor describes the balls' arrangement, but no tetrahedron face is explicitly required to lie on it. Thus the usual symmetric interpretation gives \(\mathrm{E}\), while the weaker tangent-face interpretation permits a different edge length.
